t: A Simple Way To Improve Listening
q: But the solution isn’t so difficult. In fact, with just a few simple steps you can teach your students to listen and follow your directions the first—and only—time they’re given.
After receiving their quiet attention, give the directions you want them to follow one time—which is the key the strategy.
Resist the urge to jump in and repeat yourself, cajole, or talk them through what you want them to do. Just stand in place and observe.
Slowly, leaders will emerge to either model for the others what to do or speak up and do the cajoling and repeating for you.
Students become poor listeners when they know they don’t have to listen.
When they know you’ll repeat yourself and hold their hand through every direction and every lesson, they have no reason to listen.

t: Why You Need To Draw A Line In The Sand With Difficult Students ith-difficult-students/
q: For he (or she) knows from experience that if he ratchets up his misbehavior, making it more frequent or more outrageous, the teacher will begin treating him differently.
Before long, she’ll be offering praise, prizes, and special privileges (see behavior contracts) for not disrupting the class—playing into his hands.
One of the traits that separate great teachers and classroom managers from the rest is that somewhere along the line they’ve decided not to participate in this game.
When your students know that you’ll never participate in unspoken deals, bribes, or quid pro quos, then almost magically their behavior changes.
They know that a tantrum or a dramatic stomping out of the classroom early in the year will soften the teacher up and pay dividends the rest of the way.
The only way to end the wink-wink dealmaking in your classroom, and transform your most difficult students into valued, productive citizens, is to pull the trump card out of your back pocket.

t: 3 Simple Ways To Earn Your Students' Respect https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/10/13/3-simple-ways-to-earn-your-students-respect/
q: But in the end, students can’t be persuaded or talked into respecting you. No, in this day and age, respect must be earned.
If you say it, you must follow through with it. Saying one thing and doing another is the single greatest reason why teachers struggle with disrespect.
Your students won’t respect you if you’re moody and unpredictable. Snapping at them one day and behaving as sweet as summer squash on another is confusing and disorienting to students.

When you allow students to get under your skin, it’s hard not to fall into hurtful methods like yelling, lecturing, arguing, and sarcasm—which in turn causes students to view you as a peer-equal they can backtalk, challenge, and wrest control from.
Sadly, you can no longer expect students to arrive in your classroom with a healthy respect for teachers already impressed upon their heart.
Respect is earned through the honor of your word, the steadiness of your temperament, and the gentle, quiet strength of your convictions.

t: What To Do When You Realize You've Lost Control Of Your Class ntrol-of-your-class/
q: No, the problem is that you’ve lost control of your class. But once you come to grips with this realization, once you decide you no longer want to teach in a stressful, chaotic environment, you can start doing something about it.
In fact, with the following strategy you can walk into any classroom and have the students calm and following your directions within 30 minutes.
Once you have your students seated, have them clear their desks so there are no distractions, and then simply ask them to be quiet.
Once your students are quiet, I recommend waiting in silence another five minutes after the last voice is heard.
For most classrooms, lining up to leave the room is the perfect routine because it happens every day and there are multiple opportunities for misbehavior.
Send your students back to their desks. Wait until you have their attention and respect. And then make them prove themselves once again.
